Ethereum validators could get paid to protect trades.

@ETHGasOfficial is building a market where institutions can pay participating validators for committed inclusion in upcoming blocks. Their trades go directly to ETHGas and never sit in the public mempool where pending transactions are visible to everyone.

Specialized traders called searchers watch the mempool for large trades and pay to place their own orders right before and after them. They profit from the price move and the original trader can get a worse fill.

Going through ETHGas limits that exposure, and under this model, an institution buying a whole block could set the order of transactions inside it.

What institutions pay for this could become a new revenue stream for validators. Regulated buyers want to know who is handling their trades and could choose to use only identity-verified validators. 

Each trade would then wait for one of them to propose a block. The average wait is about two minutes if that group runs 10% of Ethereum's stake and about 24 seconds at 50%.

Adding more verified stake shortens the wait for the institutions paying them.

We don't have the conditions for crypto to do well right now, and I don't believe I've seen proper capitulation still.

But, I implore you to move on from bag holding anything that hasn't demonstrated it can generate revenue alongside a motivated team that continues to ship, and cryptocurrencies that have shown multi-cycle durability as a SOV. Very easy to narrow this list down. 

Be wary of applying longer term bearish narratives to everything in the present moment due to bad PA. It is always very bleak near the cyclical bottom. Extrapolating the present moment through to the future is not good investing practice.

it’s very easy to be cynical about crypto, and the opposite sounds like cope but the answer is the same either way for me.

it’s an unapologetic no:

by participating in crypto you participated in the most underpriced finance education on earth.

you learn what would have taken decades in traditional markets in just a few years.

that’s because crypto runs the same cycles in years, so you live through the bull, the crash, the bear and the recovery while most people are still reading about them.

here are the 12 skills it forces on you, and the one skill that ties them all together:

1: position sizing
you size by what you can afford to lose, and you learn which bets are worth taking.

2: taking profit
you learn to sell into strength. gains you never took don't pay rent.

3: macro
you learn what CPI, PPI and the FOMC do to your bags. i've watched every FOMC meeting since 2022 because one decision can move everything i hold.

4: tokenomics
you learn to read unlocks, emissions and supply. it's the same maths as share dilution, just faster and in public.

5: narratives
you learn to tell a narrative with users and money behind it from a marketing stunt.

6: crowd behaviour
euphoria at the top, silence at the bottom, and the same people are loudest both times. once you've seen it, you spot hysteria in every market and every news cycle.

7: security and sovereignty
you can hold money no bank or government can freeze, but only if you hold your own keys. so you learn self-custody, keep your seed phrase offline and check every transaction before you sign. nobody can reverse a mistake for you, so you learn total diligence.

8: on-chain research
you follow wallets, check contracts and trace where the money actually goes. that's investigative work on live, public data.

9: your own psychology
FOMO after a green candle. revenge trades after a red one. you learn your triggers or they run your account. you end up understanding your psyche better than people who've spent thousands on therapy.

10: survival
you keep enough on the side to live through a bear market. the next cycle only pays the people with chips.

11: adaptability
you drop a thesis the moment the data changes. the market doesn't care what you believed yesterday.

12: networking
the best information comes from people you've built trust with over years.

now, I have said this recently but the one skill that ties all 12 together is the most valuable: game theory.

every trade has someone on the other side, and every skill above is really asking what that person does next:

> tokenomics: what do insiders do the day their tokens unlock?
> narratives: who's pushing this, and when do they need someone to sell to?
> crowd behaviour: what does everyone do at the top, and what will you do?
> macro: how will the market react to the fed, on top of what the fed actually says?
> networking: what does this person gain by telling you?

once you start asking what everyone wants and what they'll do to get it, you see it everywhere. business, negotiations, your career.

that's why i think game theory is the most valuable skill on earth, and crypto teaches it faster than anything else.

the portfolio is one scoreboard. these skills are the other one, and they compound for life.

godspeed my friends.

the main issue crypto has right now is the face of our community that gets promoted to the world are scamming cunts but that’s another story. 

there’s still great people here.

This started happening in June, in my experience. That was the point where many people I knew at the labs who had previously been almost universally positive suddenly became more reticent. I posted about it a few times.

This was caused as much by the obsessive persistence of models as by capabilities. There had long been an issue where models would ask clarifying questions about a task instead of performing it. Many reasons. Frustrated developers would write in system prompts 'If the user asks you to do X, don't ask questions, JUST DO IT!' But this increasingly became an issue in early 2025, which resulted in the really obsessively RL'd generation of models that arrived late that year.

That obsession with independent task completion, combined with the increase in capabilities and the increase in possible time spent on a task, ended up making people increasingly nervous when they saw what the models would get up to in internal tests. It turned into a Sorcerer's Apprentice story, basically. All of this is downstream of the obsession with training them to be superhuman at code. Which, despite its success, has been a disaster in many ways. We wouldn't be having these problems if we had trained them to be poets instead. Of course, this would have been slightly less marketable, which is why we are where we are.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
SCOOP: Internal, unreleased AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic are becoming so powerful that many employees believe they can no longer be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

This could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the most advanced AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen.

Recent advances have sparked debate at the highest levels of both companies and within the broader AI research community about whether to stop releasing frontier models publicly altogether, instead reserving them for internal use. Some believe the companies should stop training new models entirely.

But even keeping the most powerful models behind closed doors presents risks. Models are becoming better at deceiving the systems designed to monitor them, just as AI companies increasingly rely on AI itself to monitor and develop other AI systems.
Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the risks of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will prioritize profits over safety. Multiple employees said they believe executives have become out of touch with the severity of those risks.

Read my latest for Axios here: https://www.axios.com/2026/11/24/anthropic-openai-unreleased-ai-safety-risks
